parole.significato: To fill up with alluvial earth.
parole.testo: From Italian atterrare. Compare Late Latin atterrare (“to cast to earth”).

parole.significato: One who robs others in a lawless area, especially as part of a group.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian bandito (“outlawed”), a derivative of Italian bandire (“to ban”), from Late Latin bandīre, an alteration (due to Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌽𐌳𐍅𐌾𐌰𐌽 (bandwjan, “to signal”)) of Late Latin bannīre (“to ban”), from Frankish *bannan (“to ban”). Doublet of bandito.

parole.significato: A type of needlepoint embroidery, traditionally in wool on canvas, consisting of upright flat stitches laid in a mathem…
parole.testo: After a series of chairs found in the Bargello palace in Florence, which have a similar pattern. The palace takes its name from Italian bargello (“police headquarters”), from Late Latin barigildus, derived from the Frankish or Gothic equivalent of English borough.

parole.significato: A flat stretch of countryside; open rural plain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian campagna, from Late Latin campānia. Doublet of champagne, campaign, and campania.

parole.significato: Open country.
parole.testo: From Italian campagna, respelled after its etymon Late Latin campānia (“open country, battlefield”) (compare the region Campania), from Latin campus (“field”). Doublet of campaign, campagna, and champagne.

parole.significato: To seek; to search.
parole.testo: From Italian cercare (“to look for”), from Late Latin circāre (“to traverse, go about”), from Latin circa (“around, near, about”), circus (“a circular line or orbit”), from Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos, “circle, ring”).

parole.significato: Florid or fancy passages in vocal music.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian coloratura, from Late Latin colōrātūra, from colōrāre (“to colour”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a doge.
parole.testo: From Italian dogale (whence also Medieval Latin dogalis), from Late Latin ducalis (“ducal”). Doublet of ducal.

parole.significato: fantastic
parole.testo: From Italian fantastico (“fantastic”), from Late Latin phantasticus (“imaginary”). Doublet of fantastic and fantastique.

parole.significato: A sudden or unexpected failure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian fiasco (“bottle, flask”), from Late Latin flasca, flascō (“bottle, container”), from Frankish *flaskā (“bottle, flask”) from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ (“bottle”); see flask. “Failure” sense comes through French faire fiasco from Italian theatrical slang far fiasco (literally “to m

parole.significato: The grand end of something, especially of a show or piece of music.
parole.testo: From Italian finale (“ending”), from Late Latin fīnālis, from Latin fīnis (“end; boundary, limit”). Doublet of final.

parole.significato: A flatbread similar in style, composition, and texture to modern pizza doughs and topped with herbs, cheese and other p…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Italian focaccia, from Late Latin focācium (via its plural focācia), derived from Latin focus (“hearth”). Doublet of fougasse and pagash. Cognate with Sicilian fugazza, Serbo-Croatian pogača (“unleavened bread”).

parole.significato: The style of a prince, princess or someone of equivalent rank.
parole.testo: Calque of Italian altezza, from Late Latin altitia, from altus + -itia, equivalent to high + -ness. See highness for formation of the English term.

parole.significato: A sleeveless, knee-length vestment open at the front which is worn by Roman Catholic prelates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian mantelletta, from mantello (“cloak, mantle”) + -etta (from -etto (diminutive suffix)), probably from Late Latin mantelletum (“a short, sleeveless cape or cloak; a mantlet”). Doublet of mantlet.

parole.significato: An Italian marquis.
parole.testo: Italian, from Late Latin marchensis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to nutmeg.
parole.testo: From Italian miristico, from Late Latin myristicus (“fragrant”); the form Myristica first used by Linnaeus as a genus name for the nutmeg tree. From Ancient Greek μυριστικός (muristikós, “fragrant”), from Ancient Greek μυρίζω (murízō, “to anoint”), from μύρον (múron, “unguent, perfume”). Compare myr

parole.significato: A grandfather, especially one with Italian ancestry.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian nonno.

parole.significato: Dough made from wheat and water and sometimes mixed with egg and formed into various shapes; often sold in dried form a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian pasta (“paste; pasta, noodles”), from Late Latin pasta (“dough, pastry cake, paste”), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, “barley porridge”), neuter plural of παστός (pastós, “sprinkled with salt”), from Ancient Greek πάσσω (pássō, “to sprinkle”). Doublet of paste.

parole.significato: To perform a cursory investigation of; scope out.
parole.testo: From Italian scopo (“purpose”), from Latin scopus (“target”), from Ancient Greek σκοπός (skopós), from σκέπτομαι (sképtomai), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ-. Etymologically related to skeptic and spectrum.

parole.significato: An officer on board a merchant ship who is in charge of the cargo and its sale; also, if there are two of such officers…
parole.testo: From English supra- (prefix meaning ‘above, over’) + borrowed from Italian sopracargo, a dialectal form of sopraccarico, from sopra- (prefix meaning ‘above, over’) + carico (“cargo”) (from caricare (“to load; to take aboard”), from Late Latin carricāre, the present active infinitive of carricō (“to

parole.significato: The main part of the (human) body that extends from the neck to the groin, excluding the head and limbs.
parole.testo: From Italian torso, from Late Latin tursus, from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos, “Bacchic staff”). Doublet of thyrse, thyrsus, and torse.

parole.significato: A cloth-covered frame used for protection against rain or sun.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian ombrella (“parasol, sunshade”), from Late Latin umbrella (influenced by umbra (“shadow, shade”)), from Latin umbella, from umbra + -la (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Any of the nineteen points that divide an ordered distribution into twenty parts, each containing one twentieth of the…
parole.testo: From Italian venti (“twenty”), Late Latin vĭnti, from Latin vīgintī.

parole.significato: An expert in virtù or art objects and antiquities; a connoisseur.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian virtuoso, from Late Latin virtuōsus (“virtuous”), from Latin virtus (“excellence”). Doublet of virtuous.
